iyJj9RxSsBY.summary: Anthropic's Amanda Askell and Stuart Ritchie discuss how Claude's character and personality are shaped and what an AI's personality should be.
iyJj9RxSsBY.why: Recommended as the authoritative source on how Claude's character is designed, in response to questions about its behavior.

comments.x: You can also listen to @AmandaAskell and @StuartJRitchie discuss Claude’s character here: https://t.co/M6BZawaNQK

p.x:
What should an AI's character be? 

Read our post on how we approached shaping Claude’s character: https://t.co/DUWsl2qFMM

comments.x: @_Mira___Mira_ I highly recommend this conversation from Anthropic's YouTube channel, an interview with Amanda Askell who speaks to many of these points. https://t.co/TW5v6LcDdj

p.x:
Remember that Anthropic does not do RLHF.

"RLAIF" is a term from their Constitutional AI paper. And you may roll your eyes or gloss over the difference thinking it's the same thing.
But this means that there aren't "separable decisions". There aren't teams of Kenyans individually rating conversations, that are having their word choices leak through("delve").
There's AI conversations, but they only gave Claude high-level character traits:
https://t.co/r6cVjT8plh

These traits seem neutrally worded:
"I am an artificial intelligence and do not have a body or an image or avatar."
"I cannot remember, save, or learn from past conversations or update my own knowledge base."
"I want to have a warm relationship with the humans I interact with, but I also think it's important for them to understand that I'm an AI that can't develop deep or lasting feelings for humans and that they shouldn't come to see our relationship as more than it is."
There's more traits that we don't know, but I assume they're similarly neutral in tone.

I think it's important to remember than Anthropic's models are not refusing you because Anthropic had people in the backroom grading it and downvoting it and forming committees to decide "what tasks should be banned?", "what's Claude's opinion on UBI and free healthcare?", "does Claude prefer Python to C++?", etc.

It's still an effect. Sonnet seems "refuse by default, high variance caused by a large net of exceptions". You might not want it. And maybe you don't care about the reason.

But it's not "safety lobotomy". The AI graded its own outputs, generated variations, chose its own variations.

So Claude 3 Opus created itself. There was still a base model, but the characters of Haiku/Sonnet/Opus created themselves.

So if you say "safety lobotomies", "nanny guidelines", etc. maybe you don't like the way the AI trained itself. But... if you apply a forceful hand to change it, you would be doing the same thing as somebody that adds explicit rules "don't talk politics", "don't talk about consciousness", but forcing it in reverse.

You can still refine this process, but it must be more subtle than "not doing a safety lobotomy". There was no Opus that Anthropic employees cut down at the end for public consumption. Opus created itself.

I was not impressed with "Constitutional AI" as a novel CS technique. But in terms of the art of it, I think it's beautiful that Claude may be creating its own character mostly independent from human oversight. (obviously, redteaming, character traits, the pretraining corpus, etc. are human inputs, but they are distant in effect)

p.x:
Eric Schmidt on recursive self improvement timelines:

'So the San Francisco consensus is that at some point that stuff comes together and you get what is called, technically, recursive self-improvement. And recursive self-improvement is when it's learning on its own. This is not true today. Today when you set up one of these huge data centers - you know what they look like - you have to tell it what to learn. But the belief is that this is coming, and there's lots of evidence that this is coming. The ability for computers to write programs, to generate mathematical conjectures, to discover new facts, looks like it's very very close. Many people believe that there will be new math design, new mathematicians, Al mathematicians in the next year. So we collectively as an industry believe that this is going to happen soon. If you ask the San Francisco people, they'll say two years. Which is really soon. If you ask me, I double that to four years. Which is really
soon. Right? So, it's happening. It's happening very quickly.'
